subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 52-year-old woman with chronic low back pain describes a constant dull, throbbing ache that has persisted for several months and is not sharp or electric in character.
question: Which nerve fiber type most likely transmits this pain signal to the CNS?
explanation_correct: Nociceptive signals are carried by A-delta fibers, which transmit sharp, acute pain, and by C fibers, which transmit dull, throbbing, chronic pain. The described slow, aching, long-standing pain is characteristic of C fiber transmission. Nociceptors such as transient receptor potential vanilloid (TRPV) receptors trigger Ca2+ influx-induced Na+ channel activation to initiate these signals.

explanation_incorrect.A: A-alpha fibers are large motor and proprioceptive fibers and are not the classic carriers of dull, throbbing nociceptive pain.
explanation_incorrect.B: A-beta fibers are large touch and vibration fibers; their involvement in allodynia is discussed in neuropathic pain, but they do not transmit dull aching pain in nociceptive transmission.
explanation_incorrect.C: A-delta fibers carry sharp, acute pain, which does not match this patient's dull, throbbing, chronic description.
explanation_incorrect.E: B fibers are small myelinated autonomic preganglionic fibers, not pain-transmitting sensory fibers.

educationalObjective: Contrast A-delta fibers (sharp, acute pain) with C fibers (dull, throbbing, chronic pain).

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 61-year-old man receives intravenous morphine for pain control after an open cholecystectomy and reports substantial relief. The surgical team discusses which phases of pain transmission opioids act on.
question: Which processes of pain transmission are blocked by opioids?
explanation_correct: According to the pain transmission framework, opioids block both transmission (pain signals relayed to the CNS) and perception (the conscious appreciation of pain). Other classes that also block transmission and perception include local anesthetics (transmission only) and alpha-2 agonists; opioids do not appear on the transduction or modulation lists.

explanation_incorrect.B: Transduction is blocked by local anesthetics, alpha-2 agonists, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucocorticoids, not by opioids.
explanation_incorrect.C: Modulation is blocked by TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs, and gabapentinoids, not by opioids.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opioids block neither transduction nor modulation; transduction is covered by NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucocorticoids, and modulation by antidepressants and gabapentinoids.
explanation_incorrect.E: Including transduction in the opioid list is incorrect; transduction is targeted by anti-inflammatory and anticonvulsant-type agents, not opioids.

educationalObjective: Map opioids to the transmission and perception phases of pain processing.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 58-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis takes ibuprofen several times a day and notices reduced pain and stiffness in the inflamed joint.
question: Which process of pain transmission does NSAID therapy primarily block?

options.text: All four processes of pain transmission

explanation_correct: NSAIDs are listed among the drug classes that block transduction, the process by which noxious mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli are converted into electrical signals in nociceptors. Acetaminophen and glucocorticoids share this target; local anesthetics, alpha-2 agonists, gabapentinoids, NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucocorticoids together make up the transduction-blocking classes.

explanation_incorrect.A: Transmission is blocked by local anesthetics, alpha-2 agonists, and opioids, not by NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.B: Perception is blocked by alpha-2 agonists, opioids, TCAs, SSRIs, and SNRIs, not by NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.D: Modulation is blocked by TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs, and gabapentinoids, not by NSAIDs.
explanation_incorrect.E: No single class blocks all four processes; NSAIDs act only at the transduction step.

educationalObjective: Recall that NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucocorticoids block the transduction phase of pain transmission.

subject: Pharmacology
vignette: A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled type 2 diabetes develops symmetric burning pain, tingling, and allodynia in both feet. Nerve conduction studies confirm a distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
question: Which mechanism best explains signal propagation in this patient's neuropathic pain?

options.text: Transient receptor potential vanilloid receptor-mediated Ca2+ influx-induced Na+ channel activation triggered by thermal or chemical stimuli
Loss of descending inhibitory modulation within the dorsal horn as the primary generator of the signal
Selective demyelination of A-delta fibers with preserved C fiber function
Excessive activation of opioid receptors along ascending pain pathways
Upregulation and persistent activation of voltage-gated Na+ channels

explanation_correct: Neuropathic pain is caused by neuronal dysfunction of the CNS or PNS and is transmitted via upregulation and persistent activation of voltage-gated Na+ channels; diabetic peripheral neuropathy is the classic example. This sustained channel activity explains the spontaneous burning pain and allodynia.

explanation_incorrect.A: TRPV receptor-mediated Ca2+ influx-induced Na+ channel activation describes the initiation of NOCICEPTIVE pain from mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli, not neuropathic pain from neuronal dysfunction.
explanation_incorrect.B: Impaired descending modulation is a pharmacologic target (TCAs, SSRIs, SNRIs boost it) rather than the stated mechanism of diabetic neuropathic pain generation.
explanation_incorrect.C: Neuropathic pain here is characterized by persistent voltage-gated Na+ channel activation, not selective A-delta demyelination with C fiber sparing.
explanation_incorrect.D: Opioid receptor activation inhibits pain transmission and perception; it does not generate neuropathic pain signals.

educationalObjective: Identify upregulation and persistent activation of voltage-gated Na+ channels as the mechanism of neuropathic pain transmission.
